name: Esophageal Varices
pinyin: shí guǎn jìng mài qū zhāng
preview_text: ใน TCM อาการหลอดเลือดขอดแบบเดียวกันอาจเกิดขึ้นจากความโกรธเรื้อรัง ความอ่อนแอของระบบย่อยอาหารในระยะยาว หรือชี่และเลือดอ่อนเพลียอย่างสุดซึ้ง และแต่ละอาการต้องอาศัยพื้นฐานที่แตกต่างกัน...

synonyms: ["Enlarged Blood Vessels In The Esophagus", "Esophageal Varice", "Varicose Veins In The Esophagus"]
conventional_description: Esophageal varices are abnormally enlarged veins in the lower part of the esophagus, usually caused by portal hypertension - high blood pressure in the vein that carries blood from the digestive organs to the liver. This is most often a complication of cirrhosis, where scar tissue blocks normal blood flow. The varices themselves may not cause symptoms until they rupture, leading to life-threatening bleeding. Diagnosis is typically made through endoscopy, and the severity is graded based on size and the presence of red signs that indicate a high risk of bleeding.
conventional_treatments:
Standard treatment aims to prevent bleeding and manage acute hemorrhage. Non-selective beta-blockers are used to lower portal pressure and reduce the risk of a first bleed or rebleeding. Endoscopic variceal band ligation is performed to tie off varices and prevent rupture.
In severe or recurrent cases, a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) may be placed to reroute blood flow and decompress the portal system. Supportive care also includes managing ascites, encephalopathy, and the underlying liver disease.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the esophagus is part of the Middle Burner, intimately connected to the Liver and Spleen. The Liver stores Blood and is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body. When this flow is obstructed - often by years of stress, frustration, or poor diet - Qi and Blood stagnate, creating a back-pressure that swells the veins.
The Spleen transforms food into Qi and Blood and holds Blood within the vessels. When the Spleen is weak, it fails to manage fluids, leading to Dampness accumulation and internal pressure that further distends the veins.
These imbalances layer on top of each other. Liver Blood Stagnation is the central mechanism - the physical blockage that causes veins to engorge. When Liver Qi stagnation turns to Heat, it scorches the blood, making it thick and sticky and further weakening vessel walls. Spleen Deficiency with Dampness adds fluid retention and a heavy, bloated sensation, while Qi and Blood Deficiency leaves the veins too weak to maintain their tone. Each pattern represents a different stage or combination of these forces, and they rarely appear alone.
A rare but critical pattern is Toxic-Heat, where a sudden invasion of heat poisons the blood and can cause the fragile veins to rupture. This is an acute emergency that requires immediate Western medical intervention, but TCM can help cool the blood and stop bleeding as part of a coordinated hospital treatment. In all cases, the goal of TCM is not just to manage the varices but to correct the deeper organ imbalances that allowed them to develop.

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking about the whole picture: the quality of any discomfort, emotional state, digestion, energy levels, and any history of bleeding. Because esophageal varices often arise from liver disease, the practitioner pays close attention to signs of stagnation, heat, and weakness. The tongue and pulse provide a direct window into the inner landscape, helping to distinguish one pattern from another.
When the primary driver is Liver Blood Stagnation, the person often has a dark or greyish complexion and may feel a fixed, stabbing discomfort in the upper abdomen or chest. The tongue is dark purple or shows stasis spots, and the pulse feels wiry and choppy. This pattern is the core structural change behind the distended veins, and the diagnosis hinges on these stasis signs.
If Liver Qi Stagnation has transformed into Heat, the person is more likely to be irritable, with a bitter taste in the mouth, a flushed face, and a sensation of fullness that flares with stress. The tongue is red with a yellow coating, and the pulse is wiry and rapid. This pattern adds a layer of heat and emotional tension to the blood stasis, and the practitioner looks for these fiery clues.
Spleen Deficiency with Dampness shows up as fatigue, bloating after eating, loose stools, and a heavy sensation. The tongue is pale and swollen with tooth marks and a greasy white coating, while the pulse may feel slippery or weak. This pattern points to a digestive weakness that fails to manage fluids, creating dampness that combines with stasis and raises pressure in the veins.
In advanced or chronic cases, Qi and Blood Deficiency brings paleness, dizziness, and profound weakness. The tongue is pale with a thin coating, and the pulse is thin and weak. A rarer acute picture, Toxic-Heat, appears during a bleeding crisis, with fever, a red or purple tongue with a dry yellow coat, and a rapid pulse. These patterns require immediate professional attention.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed, stabbing pain below the ribs or in the upper abdomen", "Dark or purplish complexion, lips, or nails", "A feeling of fullness or pressure in the chest after eating", "Dark purple tongue with stasis spots, especially on the sides", "Wiry and choppy pulse"]
patterns.worse_with: Alcohol and greasy foods, Anger, frustration, and suppressed emotions, Heavy lifting or intense straining, Prolonged standing
patterns.better_with: Gentle walking or stretching, Warm, easily digested meals, Emotional calm and stress reduction, Lying on the right side with knees slightly bent
patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver stores Blood and keeps it flowing smoothly through the body. When that flow becomes stuck - often from years of emotional stress, poor diet, or chronic illness - Blood congeals and pressure builds up in the veins that drain the digestive organs into the Liver. This back-pressure forces blood to find alternate routes, causing the thin-walled veins in the esophagus to swell and twist into varices. The result is a classic picture of Blood stasis below the diaphragm, with a dark purple tongue and a wiry, choppy pulse.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body, often with purple stasis spots along the sides; sublingual veins distended and tortuous; thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè), most noticeable at the left middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Alcohol and fatty foods create Dampness and Heat that further gum up Liver Blood flow, while anger directly causes Qi to stagnate and Blood to congeal - the very mechanism of this pattern. Gentle movement and emotional ease unblock the Liver, allowing Blood to move more freely and reducing the back-pressure that swells the esophageal veins.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep meals light and warm; avoid alcohol, fried foods, and very spicy dishes, which all heat and stagnate the Liver. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps Qi and Blood flow without raising intra-abdominal pressure. Practice letting go of grudges and irritability - emotional tension is a major driver of Liver stagnation.

patterns.why_this_happens: When stress and frustration build, the Liver’s smooth flow of Qi becomes stuck. That stagnation generates heat, which rises and scorches the blood, making it thick and sluggish. Over time, the heated, stagnant blood engorges the veins in the esophagus, leading to varices. The upward pressure also causes acid reflux and a burning sensation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with redder sides, yellow coating. Pulse: wiry and rapid, especially at the left middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and anger directly stagnate Liver Qi, which then turns to heat-the very mechanism behind this pattern. Spicy, greasy, and hot foods add external heat and dampness, making the blood more sluggish and the veins more congested. Cooling foods and calming activities clear heat and smooth Qi, reducing the upward pressure that engorges the esophageal veins and soothes the burning reflux.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat more cooling, gently bitter foods like cucumber, celery, chrysanthemum tea, and dandelion greens. Avoid spicy, greasy, fried, and heavily roasted foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which add heat. Daily gentle movement-such as walking, stretching, or tai chi-helps keep Qi flowing. Make time for stress relief: deep breathing, meditation, or simply a quiet moment each day can prevent stagnation from flaring into heat.

patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, easily digestible, nourishing foods like congee, bone broth, and steamed vegetables. Avoid raw, cold, or greasy foods that further tax the Spleen. Gentle activities like tai chi or walking help Qi flow without depleting it. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture and herbs prevent variceal bleeding?
faqs.answer: TCM cannot guarantee prevention of bleeding, but by addressing the underlying patterns - moving Blood stasis, strengthening the Spleen, and clearing Heat - it may reduce the pressure and vessel fragility that lead to rupture. Many patients report fewer episodes of discomfort and improved liver function tests. However, if you have active bleeding or high-risk varices, you must follow your gastroenterologist's recommendations for banding or medication. TCM works best as a complementary approach to conventional care.

faqs.question: Is it safe to combine Chinese herbs with beta-blockers or after banding?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases, but coordination is essential. Beta-blockers lower portal pressure, and some Chinese herbs that move Blood (like Tao Ren, Hong Hua) may have mild anticoagulant effects. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your liver specialist about all treatments. After banding, herbs can help with healing and reduce recurrence, but should be started under guidance to avoid any interaction with post-procedure medications.

faqs.question: What diet changes can I make to support my liver and reduce varices?
faqs.answer: TCM dietary therapy focuses on easy-to-digest, warm, cooked foods that support the Spleen and Liver. Favour congee, soups, steamed vegetables, millet, and small amounts of lean protein. Avoid alcohol completely, as well as greasy, spicy, and fried foods that generate Dampness and Heat. Cold, raw foods weaken the Spleen and should be minimized. Eating smaller, more frequent meals can also reduce digestive pressure.

faqs.question: How quickly can I expect results from TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: Most patients notice improvements in energy, digestion, and rib discomfort within 4-6 weeks. However, the structural changes in the veins take longer - typically 2-3 months for excess patterns and 3-6 months for deficiency patterns to see stabilization on endoscopy. Consistency with herbs and acupuncture is key, and progress is monitored through symptoms, tongue, and pulse changes.

faqs.question: Will I need to take herbs forever?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. The goal is to correct the underlying imbalance so that your body can maintain stability on its own. Many patients transition from daily herbal formulas to a maintenance phase - perhaps a lower dose or a formula taken only a few days a week - after 6-12 months. However, if you have advanced cirrhosis, some herbs may be needed long-term to support liver function and prevent complications. Your practitioner will adjust the plan based on your progress.

faqs.question: Can TCM reverse cirrhosis?
faqs.answer: TCM cannot reverse established scarring (fibrosis) of the liver, but it can significantly improve liver function, reduce inflammation, and slow or halt further damage. By addressing the root patterns - Blood stasis, Dampness, and deficiency - many patients experience better energy, less fluid retention, and a lower risk of variceal bleeding. It's a supportive therapy that works alongside conventional management.

research.title: Endoscopic ligation combined with TCM syndrome differentiation for secondary prevention of esophageal variceal bleeding in liver cirrhosis
research.description: This study demonstrated that adding TCM syndrome differentiation to endoscopic variceal ligation reduced the one-year rebleeding rate and improved patient quality of life compared to ligation alone. The herbal formulas were tailored to individual patterns such as Liver Blood Stagnation and Spleen Deficiency with Dampness.
